title: HotTiles: Accelerating SpMM with Heterogeneous Accelerator Architectures
problem: Sparse matrices exhibit nonuniform patterns of nonzeros (Intra-Matrix Heterogeneity), with some regions being dense and others sparse, yet current SpMM accelerators employ identical processing elements for all regions. This results in suboptimal acceleration as the same PE type is ill-suited for both compute-bound dense and memory-bound sparse regions.
motivation: SpMM is a critical kernel across machine learning and linear algebra solvers, and the nonuniform sparsity patterns in real matrices represent an untapped optimization opportunity.
method: The paper builds a model that predicts how different types of processing chips will perform on sparse matrix multiplication, accounting for regions with different sparsity levels. It then partitions the matrix into regions and assigns each to the appropriate chip type: "Hot Workers" (optimized for heavy computation) handle dense regions, while "Cold Workers" (optimized for fast memory access) handle sparse regions. The system automatically routes each region based on its characteristics.
key_novelty: The approach uses heterogeneous processing chips rather than identical ones, routing the dense, compute-intensive regions of a sparse matrix to computation-optimized chips and the sparse, memory-intensive regions to memory-optimized chips.
contributions: Analytical modeling framework for predicting heterogeneous PE performance considering intra-matrix heterogeneity
Matrix partitioning heuristic (HotTiles) for allocating different regions to specialized processing elements
Demonstration that heterogeneous execution outperforms homogeneous approaches by 1.3-2.5x over best single worker
Validation across three different heterogeneous accelerator architectures

metrics.speedup: 9.2-16.8x vs homogeneous single-type, 1.3-2.5x vs best per-matrix worker

baselines: Homogeneous execution with only hot workers
Homogeneous execution with only cold workers
Best single worker type per matrix
limitations: Evaluation conducted via simulation rather than real hardware implementation; specific hardware fabrication constraints not discussed.
